title: Who Holds the Transcript
concept: The Alaska Court System's AI policy, version 1.2 from June, bans staff and judges from using AI on their own to make hearing notes or transcripts, then says the court's own people will soon get AI transcripts of every hearing from CourtSmart, expected by fall, labeled not the official record, linked to the official audio and restricted to internal use. The film reads that as one rule about control: close the side doors, build one front door, label what comes out. A party gets the audio through form TF-304, not the text, and the policy's stated worry is confidential information that couldn't be removed from an AI system even if a hearing was later sealed. The ink drop makes that worry felt, and the film asks whether a party should get the AI draft of their own hearing. Hero is Reels, a copper recorder with two reel eyes, and the throughline is the transcript page.

fingerprint.palette: oxblood wall panels, walnut wood, ivory sheets, brass hardware, a copper reel recorder and one cobalt ink drop
fingerprint.metaphor: a court builds one front door for its own AI transcripts and bricks up every side door, and a drop of ink in water shows why a sealed hearing can't be taken back out

palette: oxblood wall panels, walnut wood, ivory sheets, brass hardware, a copper reel recorder and one cobalt ink drop
divergence_note: The last five films were a tangerine daylight office (11-06), a night cab (11-02), an overcast moss slope (11-01), a sage chart desk (10-31) and an aubergine dusk depot (10-29). This film (with honest overlap in cream paper, brass and a cobalt accent from 10-31, and a hand and a key tag echoing 11-02) is an oxblood and walnut courtroom after hours, lit by a brass lamp and a cool green window rim, built around a copper reel recorder with a face, a glass counter that splits the frame and a macro ink drop in a tumbler of water. It has no stamp robot, cab, slope or chart desk, and its throughline is a single transcript page that is scribbled, binned, stamped, kept behind glass and finally blank.

treatment.title: The Ink Drop
treatment.summary: Explainer's pitch wins. It draws the film's hardest fact (staff inside get searchable text, the party outside gets audio, c19 against c21) as a counter window cut by glass, and carries the court's stated worry (c20) as a physical comparison, a drop of cobalt ink that can't be pulled back out of a glass of water. Grafts: the Comedian's recurring Tagalong notetaker bot sneaking in disguised (a mustache phone, a ficus), the Dramatist's bricked-up side doors and the front door lit inside the recorder, the Enthusiast's blank ribbon throughline reborn as a stamped, tethered transcript. The Enthusiast's template reading is kept as one honest aside. Hero is Reels, a new walnut recorder with reel eyes (CourtSmart as a character), not on the recent-hero list. Palette oxblood walnut, cream, brass with cobalt ink as the single accent.

angle.thesis: Alaska's court isn't banning AI transcripts, it's deciding who holds them: it bans the side doors, builds one front door inside its own recording system, labels what comes out as not the official record, and keeps it internal, a defensible first step that leaves the party with the audio and not the text.
supporting_facts: c11 c12 c13 no DIY AI hearing notes or transcripts, assistants should be removed
c14 c15 c16 the court's own CourtSmart AI transcripts of all hearings, should be ready by fall (a plan, never live)
c17 c18 c19 not the official record, links to official audio, internal only
c28 the court used AI to help format an early draft of its own policy
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: The lopsided case at full strength (c19 c21): staff and judges get searchable text of every hearing, a party gets audio by filing form TF-304. The court's stated worry (c20) is confidential information that couldn't be removed from an AI system even if a hearing was later sealed. The film leaves open whether a party should get the AI draft of their own hearing.
angle.falsifiability: False if the court treated its own transcripts like the DIY tools it bans (official record, public, cut off from the audio), or if the policy ignored its own confidentiality worry for CourtSmart.
honesty_constraints: Never say transcripts are live, launched, late or delayed, only should be ready by fall (c29 cut)
Version 1.2 June 2026, copy published by LawSites, never issued today
c20 is the policy's stated worry about hearings and AI systems, not tied to one rule
no calendar deadline from 90 and 30 days
angle.cross_challenge: Analyst 1 (enthusiast) read it as a template to copy, challenged that the 'should' provisions soften it, kept as an honest aside. Analyst 2 (public door) pressed the party-gets-audio-not-text lopsidedness, kept as the Act 3 test. Analyst 3 (strict rule) supplied the control thesis and warned CourtSmart may not solve the sealing worry, so the film claims containment not a fix. All three agreed on the falsifiable observation; the c20 attribution ambiguity was resolved by saying 'the policy's stated worry'.
